title: Shortest distances in a graph without cycles
description:
Every edge of a weighted, directed graph has an integer length, and some lengths are negative. The graph has no cycles: following edges forward never leads back to a vertex already passed. The distance from one vertex to another is the smallest total length of any path from the first to the second.

Implement a struct type called Edge with two integer fields: To, the vertex the edge enters, and Weight, its length. Then implement a function called DAGShortestDistances that receives the number of vertices, an adjacency list, and a source vertex, and returns a list holding, for each vertex, its distance from the source. Vertices are numbered from zero, and the adjacency list gives, for each vertex, the edges leaving it. Vertex numbers say nothing about the direction of the edges: an edge can lead from a higher number to a lower one.

With the edges 0->1 (length 2), 0->4 (1), 1->2 (3), 4->2 (2), 4->5 (4), 2->3 (6), 5->3 (1) and source 0:
DAGShortestDistances(6, adjacency, 0) -> [0, 2, 3, 6, 1, 5]. Vertex 2 is reached through 4 for 1 + 2 = 3, and vertex 3 through 4 and 5 for 1 + 4 + 1 = 6.

A negative edge found late can still improve a vertex that looked settled, and everything after it: with the edges 0->1 (1), 0->2 (5), 2->1 (-10), 1->3 (1) and source 0:
DAGShortestDistances(4, adjacency, 0) -> [0, -5, 5, -4].

A vertex that cannot be reached from the source gets the largest value an integer can hold, since negative numbers are real distances. With the edges 0->1 (4), 1->2 (1), 2->3 (1), 3->4 (1) and source 2:
DAGShortestDistances(5, adjacency, 2) -> [largest integer, largest integer, 0, 1, 2].

The hidden tests also check parallel edges between the same two vertices, where only the shortest one counts; graphs where every length is negative; a branch the source cannot reach that has edges into reachable vertices; and a single vertex.

This card asks for the optimal solution, and the tests enforce it: one of them is a graph of two hundred thousand vertices with negative lengths and a two second budget. Answers that keep lowering the same distance again and again as better paths turn up give the right result but are far too slow to pass. Using the fact that the graph has no cycles, every vertex and every edge has to be handled a constant number of times, so the total work stays proportional to the number of vertices plus the number of edges.
objective: Recall the linear-time way to find single-source shortest distances in a directed graph without cycles, with negative lengths allowed and unreachable vertices reported.
